column2: Phase one. Cardboard. Nobody fires back, so take your time. Learn to move, to lean, and to read the bar at the top of your screen.
Phase two. Doors. You work one room at a time, and you open the doorway from outside before you put a foot in it.
Phase three. Hallways. Doors on both sides. Every opening you walk past without slicing is an angle at your back.
Phase four. Opposition. From here on, the targets think. They slice your doorway the way you slice theirs.
Final exam. Everything at once. They learn the door that hurt them, and the walls will not stop a round. Shoot, then move.
Fundamentals. A doorway is one hundred and eighty degrees of angle. You cannot see all of it from one spot. So you walk an arc outside it, and you open it one slice at a time.
Threshold. A small room is cleared from the door. Walk the arc from one jamb to the other. Step in only for the corner you could not see.
Clean shot. The threat is behind a hostage. Do not hurry the trigger. Step sideways until the angle gives you the threat and nothing else.
Opposing doors. Slice the left, then the right, then move. Never stand between two openings you have not looked into.
Locked door. Work it from the side of the frame. Stay off the line of the doorway. That line is where the rounds come out.
Rear security. A cleared room does not stay cleared. Check behind you every time you stop.
Second look. Hands tell you more than faces. Identify at the moment of the shot, not before.
Hostage rescue. You are on a clock. Open only the angles that are on your way, and accept the ones you leave.
Home defense. Hold nothing for long. Take your shots, change position, and never fire twice from the same spot.
